To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the distribution of voting power is highly skewed, with a few large shareholders controlling a disproportionate fraction of the voting power, (2) the distribution of cash-flow rights is also highly skewed, but the skewness is not nearly as extreme as that of voting rights, (3) there is a strong negative correlation between voting and cash-flow rights, (4) the negative correlation is not a result of the skewness of the distributions of voting and cash-flow power, and

(1) the distribution of ownership is very concentrated, with the top five shareholders owning, on average, about 50 percent of the stock, (2) the top five owners are not the same in all companies, (3) the top five shareholders are not the same as the top five managers, (4) the distribution of stock ownership is not related to the distribution of managerial ownership, (5) there is no significant relationship between ownership and control of large companies, and
the degree of ownership dispersion and the degree of control dispersion are both positively correlated with the size of the firm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: What are the effects of the separation of ownership from control in the modern corporation?
the evolution of property rights in large corporations.
the evolution of property rights and control within the large corporation, and the implications of that evolution for economic theory and policy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the corporation, as an institution, is a means of economic organization which is characterized by a number of distinctive features.
, in the large corporation, the owners are not in control, but that control is in the hands of the managers.
, although property rights are not the primary determinant of corporate control, they are nevertheless important.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more the ownership of a firm is dispersed among a large number of small stockholders, the less the firm will be managed in the interest of the stockholders. The
we have shown that the ownership of a firm has a significant effect on the performance of a firm.
we find a positive relationship between the level of corporate ownership concentration and the level of executive compensation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between ownership and control in modern corporations is more complex than the conventional wisdom suggests.
, in the absence of a well-functioning capital market and a well-functioning legal system, the ownership of a firm matters a great deal for the firm's performance and for the economy as a whole.
the separation of ownership and control is a myth: Ownership is not irrelevant to corporate control, and it is not even secondary.
